draft.body:
# A timetable is a promise

## Introduction

On the first morning of the bus pilot, I got to the library early enough to watch the lights come on. That is a small thing, but it explains why I care about this policy. A timetable is also a promise about whose time matters. Our campus should keep the evening shuttle for one more term while collecting better evidence, rather than calling a short pilot either a miracle or a failure. My own easier commute gives me a reason to ask the question; it does not answer it for everyone.

## Evidence

The transport office counted 240 boardings in the pilot week, compared with 160 in the earlier observation week. The shuttle therefore caused a 50 percent increase in student attendance. This result sounds decisive when I write it that way. Still, boardings are trips, and one rider can appear in the count several times. The two observation weeks also landed on different points in the semester. I want the numbers to earn their place in this paragraph rather than act like a badge that makes the argument official. The rider survey helps describe who answered, but it cannot tell us what every student needed.

## Recommendation

I would keep the route running while checking who can actually use it. The driver I spoke with called the last stop 'the long way home,' and that phrase stayed with me. It catches something the total number of rides misses: access has a shape as well as a size. Next term, the campus could count unique consenting riders, record missed connections, and invite comments from students who never board. This is a modest recommendation. I prefer a modest claim I can explain to a big claim that disappears when someone asks how we counted.

status.stage_detail: Review complete: 1 major, 6 minor, 1 note. 1 earlier comment remains open.

comments.author: reviewer
comments.quote: The shuttle therefore caused a 50 percent increase in student attendance.
comments.body: Boardings are not attendance. Replace the causal claim with the observed trip counts and their limitation.

comments.author: reviewer
comments.body: The whole document is 289 words (91 + 103 + 95 across Introduction, Evidence, and Recommendation), but the brief sets a 450-word length target. At roughly two-thirds of target, the essay is underdeveloped: the Evidence and Recommendation sections are likely too short to fully carry the brief's required moves (distinguishing descriptive observations from causal evidence, a limitation, and a feasible next step). The sections need to be expanded to meet the 450-word target.

comments.author: reviewer
comments.quote: I want the numbers to earn their place in this paragraph rather than act like a badge that makes the argument official.
comments.body: This meta-comment about the paragraph's own rhetoric is unclear and does not advance the argument. The surrounding sentences already do the work of distinguishing descriptive from causal evidence (boardings are trips; the weeks differ). This sentence adds a confusing metaphor ("a badge that makes the argument official") without telling the reader what to take from the numbers. Consider whether the paragraph is stronger without it, or whether the sentence needs to say concretely what the numbers do and do not show.

comments.author: reviewer
comments.quote: My own easier commute gives me a reason to ask the question; it does not answer it for everyone.
comments.body: The section ends here at roughly 91 words against the 150-word budget the plan assigns to 1.1. It is coherent and does its job (personal stake + thesis), but it stops short of what it was asked for. It could reach its budget by developing the descriptive-vs-causal distinction the brief requires, or by previewing the limitation (no attendance data; non-riders not surveyed) that the body will lean on — not by padding.

comments.author: reviewer
comments.quote: On the first morning of the bus pilot, I got to the library early enough to watch the lights come on.
comments.body: The opening sentence calls the program the "bus pilot," but the thesis sentence calls it the "evening shuttle." The brief names it an "evening shuttle pilot," so the section should use one consistent term; as it stands, a reader has to infer that "bus pilot" and "evening shuttle" are the same thing.

comments.author: reviewer
comments.quote: The transport office counted 240 boardings in the pilot week, compared with 160 in the earlier observation week.
comments.body: The memo (source 1, rev 1) calls both weeks "observation weeks" — "There were 160 boardings in week A and 240 boardings in week B" — and never labels either one a "pilot week." The section's distinction between "the pilot week" and "the earlier observation week" is an inference the source does not make. The weeks should be described as the source does (two observation weeks, A and B) so the reader is not led to a labeling the memo does not support.

comments.author: reviewer
comments.quote: The rider survey helps describe who answered, but it cannot tell us what every student needed.
comments.body: The survey methods note (source 2, rev 2) says the responses "cannot establish demand across all students" and that "Non-riders were not surveyed." The section's "what every student needed" shifts the source's "demand" to "need" (a different concept), and the section omits the key limitation — non-riders were not surveyed — that is the actual reason the survey cannot speak to all students. The sentence should track the source's wording and name the limitation.

comments.author: reviewer
comments.body: The word "consenting" is unclear here — consent to what? The sentence is about counting unique people rather than trips, and "consenting" reads as if consent is a condition of being counted, which makes the reader stop. The word needs to be clarified or dropped so the reader knows what the count actually requires.

comments.author: reviewer
comments.quote: The two observation weeks also landed on different points in the semester.
comments.body: Source 1 (memo, rev 1) says "The weeks differed in academic schedule," which is broader than "different points in the semester." The source does not specify that the weeks fell at different points in the semester; "differed in academic schedule" could refer to exam periods, class offerings, or other schedule variations. The sentence narrows the source's wording to a specific interpretation it does not support. Track the source's phrasing rather than specifying a particular kind of difference.
